Ilse realises that the problem is the noise of their boots, and the answer is already in her bag. She remembers the thick woollen socks that her grandmother knitted for her, and a very small smile starts on her face.
Ilse takes off her boots, hands Tamsin a spare pair of thick socks, and whispers that this is what she packed them for. Tamsin pulls them on over her stockings and grins in the moonlight like a cat.
In their thick woollen socks, the two girls glide across the marble like ghosts. They stop whenever a heron looks their way, and they move again whenever the clicking carries them past.
They slip between two herons whose long beaks swing past with a faint whirr, only a few inches from their heads. Ilse can see her own pale face reflected in the glass of an eye.
The glow from Ilse's tiny lamp catches the glass eye of a heron and makes it flash. She covers the lamp with her hand at once, and Tamsin steadies her elbow and does not breathe.
A heron steps straight toward the girls and stops with one brass foot raised above Tamsin's head. Ilse stares at the foot, which could crush a girl's hand, and then the heron clicks on past.

Halfway across, Ilse's tea tin begins to rattle in her bag, and Tamsin catches it just in time with both hands. They reach the far door at last, slip through, and close it behind them without a click.

Behind the door a shorter stair winds up into the roof of the tower, and the clicking of the herons fades behind them. At the top is a small landing and a heavy wooden door with a faint line of light under it.
The topmost room is round and silent, and heavy velvet curtains hang over every window. In the middle stands a carved wooden stand, and on it lies a grey book under a glass cover.
A ring of twelve tiny silver bells hangs around the glass, and each one is fastened to a hair-thin wire. The wires run to the rim of the glass cover, and they shine like spider threads.
Ilse studies the ring and works out how it must work. If anyone lifts the glass, the wires will tug, the bells will ring, and the herons will come clattering up the stairs.
Ilse looks at the bells for a long time, and the beginnings of an idea unfold in her mind. A bell that cannot swing cannot ring, she thinks, and tying a thread is exactly what a mender does best.
Ilse takes out her finest silk thread and cuts twelve short lengths with her tiny scissors. She asks Tamsin to hold the candle steady, and Tamsin grips it in both hands like a holy relic.

With the steadiest fingers she owns, Ilse slips a loop of silk around the clapper of the first bell and ties a tiny knot. The bell trembles, but it makes no sound, and she lets out a breath she has been holding for a minute.
A draught from a crack in the wall sets the fourth bell trembling, and the candle flame leans over. Ilse catches the bell between two fingers and holds it perfectly still until the air calms down.
Bell by bell the work goes on, and the minutes crawl past like snails. Tamsin, who cannot bear the tension, bites her lip until it is nearly raw, but the candle never moves.
Ilse ties a loop around the twelfth and last bell, and she draws the knot closed with one quiet tug. The whole ring of bells hangs as mute as pebbles, and it has taken her nearly an hour.
Ilse and Tamsin take hold of the glass cover and lift it together, as slowly as two snails climbing a wall. The twelve bells sway on their wires, but not one of them makes a sound.
Ilse undoes the silver clasp and opens the great grey book, and she turns page after heavy page. Under the candle every leaf is blank, as white and silent as new snow.

Tamsin whispers in dismay that they have been tricked and that the book is empty. Ilse touches the paper, notices a faint silvery sheen on it, and understands that the ink must wake only under the light of the moon.
Tamsin reaches for the curtain, but Ilse stops her hand. From the outside the windows are mirrors, and a window that suddenly lit up would flash a signal to every patrol boat on the sea.

Ilse decides that there is no time to copy anything, and that a copy made by candlelight would be blank in any case. The whole book must go with them, and they must read it on the barge, in the moonlight.
They wrap the Atlas in a heavy cloth that Tamsin finds under the stand, and they knot the corners into a sling. It weighs as much as a small dog, and they have to carry it between them.

They are almost at the door when a glow of lamplight creeps under it, and a deep, unhurried tread begins to climb the stairs. It is Corvin Ashgrove himself, who has come, as he always does, to read his Atlas by the light of the full moon.

Ilse and Tamsin dive behind the nearest heavy curtain, hugging the Atlas between them and praying that the cloth will not rustle. Behind it they find a narrow wooden door, and Ilse recognises it from a cluster of tiny holes on the thief's map.

The Harbour Lord strides in with his velvet cloak swinging, puts his lamp on the floor and pulls back the curtains one by one. A flood of moonlight pours into the round room, and the glass of the windows blazes like silver.

While the Harbour Lord hums at his window, Ilse eases the narrow door open and the girls slip through with the heavy bundle. Then she hears the humming stop, and she knows that he is looking at the empty stand.

Through the crack in the door Ilse sees the Harbour Lord stop in the middle of the room and stare at the empty stand. Slowly his eyes move to the ring of bells, each one tied with a neat little knot of silk.

The Harbour Lord throws back his head and roars with such fury that the windows tremble in their frames. Far below, a dozen mechanical herons snap their heads up at once and begin to stalk toward the stairs.

The herons pour up the main stairs in a clattering river, and the Harbour Lord storms out of the room to meet them. Ilse and Tamsin do not wait to see more, and they creep down the narrow wall stair as fast as they dare.
The narrow stair ends in a small door behind a pillar in the corner of the great hall. The hall is empty and white with moonlight, because every heron has rushed up the stairs after the Harbour Lord.
The girls run across the polished marble in their stockinged feet, with the heavy Atlas bumping between them. Tamsin slips and goes down on one knee, and Ilse hauls her up without dropping the sling.

Behind them a clatter changes direction, and the herons wheel round and come thundering back down the stairs into the hall. Their eyes burn red, and their brass legs scissor across the marble faster than any person can run.

Ilse and Tamsin plunge down the spiral stairs with the Atlas between them, and the herons clatter at their backs like an avalanche of cutlery. Ilse counts the steps aloud, because the counting is the only thing that is keeping her upright.
A white cross shines on the wall in the moonlight, and Ilse screams that it is the forty-first step. She leaps as high as she can, and Tamsin follows her without a word.

The herons, which know nothing about painted planks, charge straight onto the false step and crash through in a bright cascade of brass. A long splash echoes up from far below, and the clattering stops all at once.
The girls tumble down the last stairs and through the dark cellar into the damp passage at the bottom of the tower. Tamsin slams the iron door behind them and jams her spanner through the handle.

Ilse and Tamsin throw themselves into the little boat and row like people pursued by thunder. Behind them a great lantern is lowered into a fast black boat, and a voice they know all too well bellows across the water.
Ilse snatches up the signal lantern and flashes it three times toward the dark sea, her hands shaking badly. Far out beyond the rocks a single light winks back, as steady as a star.

At the barge, Fenwick hauls the girls aboard with one enormous hand apiece, then lifts the heavy bundle like a loaf. Barnaby shouts from the bow that the tide is turning, and Old Puffin begins to roar.
The whole crew wants to hear everything at once, and the questions fly like gulls. Fenwick wraps the girls in blankets and gives them tea, and Captain Brae silently touches Ilse's shoulder.
On the open deck, under a moon as round as a coin, Ilse sets the Atlas on a barrel and opens the silver clasp. The whole crew gathers round and holds its breath.

The pages wake one by one with delicate lines of silver, as if someone were drawing them from underneath. Every channel of the Whisperreef appears at once, along with arrows for the tide and tiny notes for every shoal.

Barnaby, who cannot see a single line of it, leans over the pages with his face turned to the moon. He says that he can smell the sea being made plain at last, and nobody laughs, because everyone knows exactly what he means.

Ilse finds the Tide-Gate on the silver page, with a tiny drawing of a clock beside it that shows the hour it will open. The tide will be at its lowest in about an hour, and after that the gate will not open again for a long time.

A fast black boat slips away from the jetty with a great lantern, and Barnaby hears its oars on the water. Captain Brae calls for every scrap of steam, and Tamsin dives into the engine room like a diver.

The black boat is far quicker than the barge, and the gap between them closes with every minute. Soon the Harbour Lord is close enough for Ilse to see the rings on his fingers as he cups his hands to shout.

The Harbour Lord calls across the narrowing water in a voice as smooth as warm butter. He offers Ilse a fine house, a salary beyond counting and the title of Chief Mapmaker, if she will simply hand back the Atlas.

The Harbour Lord adds that his clerk has already torn up her licence notice, and that her little shop will be safe for ever. He sounds like a man who has never been refused anything, and who finds kindness cheap when he holds every card.
For a moment Ilse is truly tempted, because she can picture it all so clearly. A quiet study high in a tower, endless ink and paper, a door with a lock, and no more tides or herons or thieves.
Ilse thinks of Wren eating his bun as though he had not seen food for days. She thinks of Mistress Pim's ovens and of the thin faces on Captain Brae's island, and the quiet tower seems to shrink.
Ilse stands at the rail with the Atlas in her arms and says that a map belongs to everyone who must cross the water. For once in her life, her voice does not tremble at all.
The smile drops from the Harbour Lord's face like a plate, and he orders his oarsmen to row harder. No harbour will ever take the barge again, he shouts, and her captain will never sail again.
Barnaby says that the gate is close, and he can smell the old stone. Ilse checks the Atlas, and the little silver clock tells her that the doors will open in less than a quarter of an hour.
Tamsin pushes Old Puffin far past what is safe, and the steam screams in every pipe. The barge leaps forward like a startled horse, and Fenwick shovels coal until his shirt is black.

Guided by the silver lines, the barge reaches the Tide-Gate at the exact minute that the water has fallen low enough. The great doors swing slowly apart with a groan, and moonlight pours through the gap.

They shoot through with an arm's length to spare, and the old stones grind shut behind them with a boom across the reef. The Harbour Lord's boat, a heartbeat too late, is left drifting before a closed gate and a very long tide.

Beyond the gate the sea is calm and wide, and the Atlas shows a safe channel curving out around the reef. Ilse sits down beside the barrel to check it once more, and she is asleep with the book in her lap before she has finished.
At dawn the green hump of Kettle Island lifts out of the sea, with gulls wheeling above it. Fenwick wakes Ilse with a mug of ginger tea, and she sits up to look, blinking like an owl.
At the end of the stone pier stands a crowd of thin, tired people, shading their eyes against the light. They have seen no ship for so long that for a while nobody dares to cheer.
Captain Brae leaps onto the pier before the barge has stopped, and she wraps her arms around a small grey-haired woman in a patched shawl. For a long time, neither of them says a single word.
Hester Brae is thin and tired, but she is quite safe and very happy. Ilse, standing awkwardly on the deck with her hands clasped, discovers that her own eyes are wet as well.

Fenwick carries every sack of oats and flour from the barge onto the pier and lights a fire under an enormous pot. The thin children line up with their bowls, and they eat until they cannot eat any more.

Watching the quay, Ilse knows that a single book on a single barge cannot save an island. It must be copied for every boat and every captain, she realises, and she must begin before the Harbour Lord arrives.
Ilse sets up a table on the pier at moonrise, and the islanders bring her paper, ink and every candle they own. Hester Brae stirs crushed shell into the ink until it shines silver in the moonlight.
By midnight a dozen hands are helping her, and each one has been taught to copy a single channel. The first neat copy is drying in the wind, and Ilse holds it up to the moon like a newborn child.
In four days the islanders make hundreds of copies, each one drawn in silver ink under the moon. Every fishing boat in the harbour gets one, tucked into its cabin like a good-luck charm.

Captain Brae raised her brass spyglass, held it to her eye for a long moment and then lowered it with an expression like a closing door. Out of the mist behind them came a sleek cutter flying the Harbour Lord's flag, its oars flashing in perfect time and its name, Sparrowhawk, gleaming in gold letters on the bow. Somebody had known where they were going, and somebody had come to stop them.

The crew looked at the sealed gate and then at the cutter, and nobody needed to say aloud that they were trapped. Old Puffin, however bravely she wheezed, was far too slow to outrun a ship with forty oars, and the tide was still a good hour from its lowest point. Fenwick, who had stopped chewing for the second time in his life, laid down the ladle with great solemnity.

A thin, stern voice rang across the water through a speaking trumpet, commanding the barge to heave to in the name of the Harbour Lord. It belonged to Lieutenant Slate, who stood at the bow of the Sparrowhawk with his hands behind his back like a statue of a disappointed schoolmaster. Tamsin, paying him no attention whatsoever, flung another shovelful of coal into Old Puffin, and the little funnel began to shake with smoke.

Ilse's eye, trained by years of reading the smallest marks, caught a single pinhole set apart from the others and pointing to a gap between two black rocks. It was barely wide enough for the barge, and no sensible sailor would have tried it, but she put her finger on the paper and asked the captain to trust her. Captain Brae looked at her for one long breath and then spun the wheel.

The barge scraped through the gap with scarcely a hand's breadth to spare on either side, while Tamsin held her breath and Barnaby counted the seconds under his own. Behind them the cutter, which had followed too eagerly, struck a sandbar that the thief had marked long ago and stuck fast, its crew tumbling across the deck like skittles. Nobody on the barge had the heart to cheer until the last of the black rocks had slid past, and then they cheered so hard that Crumb fell off the mast.

The crew gathered at the stern to look back at the stranded cutter, where Lieutenant Slate stood on the tilted deck shaking his fist at the sky. The rising tide would float her free in a few hours, Captain Brae said, but by then the barge would have a long head start, and a head start was all that she had ever hoped for. Tamsin turned a somersault on the deck, to the great alarm of the gull.

The scrape in the narrow gap had sprung a small leak in the hull, and Tamsin and Fenwick set about it at once, pressing a patch of canvas and hot tar over the damaged plank. Ilse held the lamp, and noticed with quiet pride that her hands, which had trembled all morning, were now as steady as a surgeon's. The barge, she thought, was a lot like a map, in that almost anything could be mended if somebody cared enough to try.

As evening fell the barge anchored beside a low sandbar that Barnaby called the Pale Bar, and the crew gathered driftwood and lit a small fire in a hollow of the sand. Its flames leaned in the wind, and the smoke smelled of salt and old ships, and Ilse held out her hands to it with a gratitude she had never felt toward a fire in her own tidy grate. Above the dark reef the sky was slowly turning the colour of a ripe peach, and the first star had come out over the water.

Fenwick served a thick fish stew in dented tin bowls, flavoured with herbs that he refused to name, and the crew ate in a contented silence broken only by the clink of spoons. Crumb the gull hopped among the boots, stole a crust from Barnaby's bowl, and was forgiven at once, since nobody had the energy to argue with a creature that had only one leg. Ilse, who had never in her life eaten supper out of doors, decided that it improved the taste enormously.

As the fire sank low, Barnaby told the old story of Jory Lightfoot, who had climbed into the Glass Tower in the days before the Harbour Lord's grandfather owned it. Jory never stole the Atlas, the story went; he found it blank under his lantern, and he was far too clever to carry off a book that he could not read. Instead he charted the way in and hid the chart for some honest hand to find, and nobody knew whether this was true, but nobody wished to say so.

Ilse sat wrapped in a borrowed blanket with her chin on her knees, staring so hard into the flames that her eyes watered. At last she confessed, in a small and careful voice, that she had never been so frightened in all her life, and that she was holding herself together with nothing but tea and politeness. Nobody laughed, and Fenwick quietly refilled her mug without a single word of comfort, which was exactly the right kind.

The captain, staring at the flames, answered that she was frightened too, for her mother still lived on Kettle Island and had sent no word for three weeks. She said it in the same flat voice in which she had described the reef, and it was this, more than any speech, that told Ilse how heavily it weighed. It was the moment when Ilse understood that the journey was about people and not about paper.

Captain Brae drew a scrap of knotted net from her pocket and turned it over in the firelight, saying that her mother, Hester, had taught her to mend nets before she could read. Any knot in the world could be undone, Hester used to say, as long as the hand that picked at it was patient. Ilse, who had spent her life picking at the knots of old paper, felt a sudden warmth toward a woman she had never met, and it seemed to her that mending ran in both families.

Ilse gazed up at a sky so crowded with stars that it seemed to hum, and she thought of her warm shop, her cold teapot and her locked door, and waited for the great wave of longing that she expected. It did not come, and instead she felt something small and fierce, like an ember under ash, which told her that she would go on. She would go on, she thought, to the very end of the thing, and she would very likely complain all the way.

At dawn the rising tide lifted the barge gently from the sand, and the crew hauled up the anchor and shoved off into the pale morning, with Old Puffin muttering in her engine room. Ilse folded her borrowed blanket into a perfect square, corner to corner, and laid it on the bunk, and Fenwick remarked that in thirty years of cooking on boats he had never seen a neater one. It was a very small thing, she thought, but a person has to begin somewhere.

The morning was calm and clear, and the barge slid between low rocks as quietly as a thought, with Ilse at the bow reading the pinholes aloud in a steady voice. The crew had stopped asking her whether she was sure, which was the highest compliment they could have paid her, and she realised with a small jolt that she was. There was no sign of the cutter anywhere, though Barnaby kept turning his head to listen for it.

Barnaby lifted his nose to the wind, sniffed twice and announced that he could smell cold stone and old woodsmoke, the smell of a place where fires were lit by men who did not like visitors. Skerry Hollow must be close, he said, and he asked Ilse to read the next hole as slowly and as plainly as she could. Everyone on the barge fell quiet, even the one-legged gull, which had been muttering to itself all morning.

By afternoon the barge reached Skerry Hollow, a lonely black rock out of which the Glass Tower rose in a slender spire of mirrored windows. It looked as if some giant had planted a splinter of the sky on the ocean and forgotten to take it away. Somewhere inside, Ilse thought with a dry mouth, lay the book that a hungry island needed.

Every pane flashed in the sun like an eye, and Ilse felt as if the whole building were watching the small barge creep toward it. Captain Brae, who had the same feeling and acted on it more quickly, ordered the sail lowered and the barge tucked into a narrow cove behind a ridge of rock. There, out of sight of every mirror, the crew held their breath and waited for something to happen, and nothing did.

Captain Brae raised her spyglass and counted two patrol boats circling the island at a lazy pace, with a guard hut crouching at the end of a stone jetty and a lamp burning in its window. High in the tower, behind one pane, something metal glinted in the sun, and she remarked, in a carefully ordinary voice, that it was probably only a bird. Nobody on the barge believed her for a moment, and Ilse felt her stomach turn over slowly, like a pancake in a pan.

Spread on a crate, the thief's map revealed what no honest chart could, a small drain door at the foot of the tower, hidden just above the waterline and reached only at low tide. A bundle of tiny holes behind it marked a staircase winding upward, and beside the topmost holes Jory had pricked a tiny crescent moon. Ilse put her finger on the crescent and said, very softly, that this was where the Atlas lived.

The crew argued for a quarter of an hour about who should go into the tower, and the captain, who was not accustomed to staying behind, argued loudest. In the end the sums were against her, for only Ilse could read the thief's map, only Tamsin could open any lock ever made, and somebody had to keep the barge ready for a quick escape. Captain Brae folded her arms, scowled at the tower for a long time, and then gave way with the grace of a cat being carried out of a warm room.

Barnaby pointed to the pale shape that already hung over the eastern rocks and said that by midnight the moon would be full. The Atlas, he reminded them, showed its ink only in moonlight, and so the Harbour Lord always opened it on the night of a full moon, at his window, with nobody to watch. They would have to be in the tower and out again before he arrived, and Ilse did the sum twice and did not like the answer.

Fenwick wrapped a pile of oatcakes in a clean cloth, Tamsin rolled her lock wires into a leather case with the solemnity of a surgeon, and Barnaby oiled the oars of the little rowing boat. Ilse laid out her spool of silk thread, her tiny shaded lamp and a spare pair of woollen socks, counted them, and then counted them again. It occurred to her that she had never prepared for a burglary before, and that the tea tin had better come too.

As the sun sank red behind the reef, the captain went through the plan a final time, in the voice of a woman who was trying not to sound afraid. Ilse and Tamsin would row ashore after dark, find the drain door, reach the Atlas and return, and the barge would answer three flashes of a lantern with a single flash of its own. Ilse said that it was a thoroughly bad plan, and then she agreed to it.

As dusk deepened, Ilse and Tamsin climbed down the rope ladder into the little rowing boat, and the crew leaned over the rail to whisper their good luck. Fenwick pressed one last bun into Ilse's hand, Barnaby touched her sleeve as though to fix her in the world, and the captain simply nodded, which was somehow the finest farewell of all. Then the barge was a dark shape behind them, and the oars dipped into the water with a sound like someone stirring a cup.

The two of them rowed across the darkening water toward the black bulk of Skerry Hollow, with the moon climbing slowly behind them like a lantern held by a patient giant. The oars were heavy and rough, and after a dozen strokes Ilse's palms had blistered, though she said not a word about it. Tamsin, who rowed as easily as other people breathe, kept a steady rhythm and hummed a tune about a miller's daughter.

A strong current suddenly seized the little boat as though it wanted to carry it back to the open sea, and for a few terrible moments they spun sideways with the rock sliding away on the left. Ilse shielded her tiny lamp with a hand, bent over the map and found a faint mark that showed a back eddy curling in toward the rock. She pointed, Tamsin pulled, and the water, which a moment before had been their enemy, turned and pushed them gently home.

Between them they brought the boat against the slippery rock and tied it to an old iron ring set into the stone, Tamsin tying a knot that Fenwick himself would have admired. Ilse, shaking and soaked to the knees, discovered that she was prouder of her blisters than she had ever been of her ink. It was a strange feeling, and she resolved to think about it later, in a chair.

Around the corner of the rock came a patrol boat, its lantern swinging at the bow and its guards yawning at the oars. The girls pressed themselves flat into the shadow of an overhanging ledge, and the golden light slid across the stone a hand's breadth above their heads, paused, and passed on. Ilse discovered that it is possible to be entirely rigid and entirely terrified without making a single sound.

When the patrol boat had gone, Tamsin admitted in a whisper that she was frightened too, although she had never said so aloud to anyone on the barge. Ilse, who had been brought up to believe that most troubles could be improved by food, broke Fenwick's last bun in half and gave her the larger piece. They ate in the dark, side by side, and felt a good deal braver than they had a minute earlier.

The tide was low, which gave them a ledge, and the two of them edged along it with their backs to the cliff and the waves slapping hungrily at the rock a yard beneath their boots. Seaweed clung to their ankles like wet string, and the stone was so slimy that Tamsin remarked, in a whisper, that it had been coated in soap by the Harbour Lord's own hand. Ilse, who counted every step because it kept her mind off the sea, reached sixty-two and stopped.

The drain door was rusty and slimy with weed, so low that a grown man would have had to crawl, and Tamsin knelt before it with her leather case open on the rock. She coaxed its ancient lock with two slender wires and a murmured tune, while Ilse held the lamp in both hands and tried to remember when she had last breathed. After what felt like a year, the lock gave up the struggle and surrendered with a faint, grateful click.

The door groaned open on a passage so low that the girls had to crawl, and it smelled of seaweed and cold stone, with water dripping somewhere in the dark. Tamsin closed the door softly behind them, shutting out the moon, and for a moment they could see nothing at all. Ilse held the map close to her chest and whispered that the first turn was to the left.

The passage ended in a vast stone cellar, crowded to the rafters with sacks of flour, crates of salted fish and barrels of oil, every one stamped with the marks of Kettle Island's boats. Tamsin read the stamps in the weak lamplight, then turned to Ilse with a face that was white with fury. This was the island's food, and the Harbour Lord had been sitting on it, like a dragon on gold, while the children grew thin.

Tamsin wanted to start hauling the sacks to the boat that very minute, and it took all of Ilse's quiet persuasion to remind her that two girls could not carry a cellar. She promised, with a firmness that surprised them both, that the island would have every sack back, and she wrote a tiny note about the cellar in the margin of the map. It was the first time she had ever made a promise in pencil and meant it in ink.

On the far side of the cellar the thief's map showed a small oak door, and when Tamsin eased it open they found the foot of a narrow staircase winding upward inside the wall of the tower. Jory Lightfoot had pricked a hole for every step, and Ilse, who could not look at a row of anything without counting it, reached one hundred and twelve before she had finished the first breath. It was, she said faintly, a great many stairs for a person who normally stayed on one floor.

At the twentieth step a narrow slit in the wall gave onto the night, and they paused to look through glass that was clear from this side and, Ilse realised, a mirror from the other. The whole sea lay below, silver and still beneath the climbing moon, with the small dark shape of the barge crouched behind its rock like a patient animal. Tamsin lifted a hand and waved at it silently, and Ilse found that she had a lump in her throat.

Somewhere near the thirty-eighth step something stirred in the back of Ilse's memory, like a fish turning in deep water, and she stopped so suddenly that Tamsin walked into her. Before they left the barge she had seen a tiny cross pricked beside the staircase holes, and she had dismissed it as a speck of dust. A mender does not dismiss specks, however, and her blood began to run cold.

Just before the forty-first step Ilse snatched Tamsin by the collar and held her back with both hands, and Tamsin's boot hung in the air a finger's breadth above the stair. In the lamplight the step looked like worn grey stone, but as Ilse held the lamp lower she saw the faint grain of a wooden plank showing through the paint. It had been painted, with great skill and some malice, to look exactly like everything around it.

Tamsin, white to the lips, dropped a small coin onto the painted plank, which tipped neatly like a drawbridge and let the coin fall away into the darkness. For a long moment there was nothing at all, and then, from somewhere very far below, they heard the faintest of splashes. Neither of them said a word, and Tamsin buttoned her coat up to the chin as though it might protect her.

Tamsin fished a stub of chalk from her pocket and marked a bold cross on the wall beside the false step, so that they would not forget it on the way down. Then they stretched across the gap one at a time, holding hands over the empty darkness, and landed safely on the forty-second step with their hearts thumping. Ilse noticed that her legs, which had been shaking, had suddenly decided to take charge.

At the eightieth step the girls sat down to rest, and Ilse examined her blistered palms with the severe expression of a surgeon inspecting a bad mend. Somewhere above them, very faint and very regular, came a sound like a clock being wound, over and over, in a large and empty room. Tamsin held a finger to her lips and said that she did not think it was a clock.

The clicking grew louder with every step, until it seemed to fill the stairwell like the beating of a giant's heart, and at last the staircase ended in a tall archway full of white light. The girls crept up the last of the one hundred and twelve steps on their hands and knees, and Ilse, who had never in her life peered around a corner without good reason, peered around the corner. What she saw there caused her to forget the number she had been counting, and very nearly her own name.

At the top of the stairs lay a great moonlit hall where a dozen metal herons patrolled on thin brass legs, each step marked by a precise, whirring click. The Warden Herons turned their long necks toward every sound, however small, and their glass eyes burned briefly red as they listened. Ilse pressed herself against the pillar and wondered how any thief, however famous, had ever walked through such a room.

The hall was enormous, floored with squares of black and white marble like the board of some giant's game, and held up by pillars as thick as ancient oaks. Moonlight poured through the tall windows in long white bars, and through those bars the herons wandered in slow circles, their brass legs flashing and their long necks swaying. The whole room ticked, whirred and clicked like the inside of a watch, and Ilse felt like a tiny speck lost among the wheels.

Tamsin watched the herons for a long minute with the narrowed eyes of an engineer, and she whispered that every one of them moved in time to a steady click, like a pendulum in a clock. The tick itself never stopped, she said, but the moment any other noise broke into it, the nearest heron froze, swung its head round and listened. It was a machine built to hear a mouse sneeze from the far end of the hall, and to punish the mouse severely.

Ilse's boot scraped against the stone with a sound no louder than a whisper, and the nearest heron whipped its head around, its glass eyes burning a deep and angry red. The two girls became statues, with Ilse balanced on one foot like a flamingo, and the heron stared at the space where they stood for what felt like a week. At last the red faded, the neck turned away, and the whole room resumed its patient ticking.

Ilse realised that the trouble lay in the sound of their boots on stone, and as she realised it her hand crept toward the bag on her shoulder, where three pairs of thick woollen socks lay folded. Her grandmother had knitted them with the words that one never knew when a warm foot might be needed, and Ilse had always thought it one of the old woman's odder remarks. A very small, very private smile began to spread across her face, and she reached into the bag at once.

Ilse drew off her boots, pulled on a pair of thick woollen socks and handed Tamsin a spare pair, whispering that this was exactly what she had packed them for. Tamsin dragged them on over her own stockings, grinning in the moonlight like a cat who has been offered a second dinner. They tied their boots round their necks by the laces, and both of them looked quite ridiculous.

In their thick socks the girls glided across the marble like two ghosts in a dancing school, pausing whenever a heron looked their way and sliding forward again when the clicking carried it past. Ilse had never moved so carefully in her entire life, not even when carrying a full teapot across a crowded room. The map told her that the door was on the far side of the hall, and the hall, she discovered, was a good deal wider than it looked.

They slipped between two herons whose beaks swung past with a faint whirr only a few inches from their heads, close enough for Ilse to feel the cool air of the passage on her cheek. In the polished glass of one great eye she could see her own face, pale, wide-eyed and quite unrecognisable as the face of a woman who mended maps. She wondered whether, if she had thought of this in the shop, she would have chosen a quieter sort of week.

The glow from Ilse's tiny lamp touched the glass eye of a passing heron and made it flash like a star, and she covered the light with her hand so fast that she scorched her palm. Tamsin steadied her elbow, and both of them stood motionless in the thin moonlight as the bird tilted its head, considered the matter and moved on. Ilse put the lamp out altogether and decided that the moon could do the rest.

A heron stalked straight toward the girls, its thin legs flashing, and stopped over Tamsin with one brass foot raised just above her head. Ilse stared at that foot, which could have crushed a hand like an egg, and counted the clicks of the clock inside it, one, two, three, four. On the fifth the foot came down a yard away, and the heron went clicking on into the moonlight.

Halfway across, Ilse's tea tin began to rattle in her bag with a sound like a tiny cymbal, and Tamsin caught it with both hands a split second before the nearest heron turned its head. They reached the far door at last and slid through, closing it behind them so softly that even the latch seemed to hold its breath. Then the two of them leaned against the wall and laughed silently, shaking all over, until the tears ran down their faces.

Behind the far door a shorter and steeper stair wound up into the very roof of the tower, and the whirring of the herons faded behind them until it was only a murmur. At the top lay a small landing and a heavy wooden door, with a thread of pale light lying along the bottom of it like a line of chalk. Ilse put her ear against the wood, heard nothing but her own pulse, and eased the latch open.

The topmost room was round and silent, with heavy velvet curtains drawn across every window, so that only a thin silver seam showed where the moon was pressing at the cloth. In the very middle stood a carved wooden stand, and on it, beneath a bell of glass, lay a thick grey book with a silver clasp. It was so much smaller than Ilse had imagined that for a moment she wondered if they had come to the wrong room.

Around the glass hung a ring of twelve tiny silver bells, each fastened to a wire so fine that it shone like a spider's thread in the light of Tamsin's candle. The wires ran down to the rim of the cover and into small holes in the stand, and the moment Ilse saw them she understood the entire arrangement. It was the sort of invention that a very clever and very unpleasant person would be proud of.

Ilse studied the arrangement for a minute and worked out how it must function. If anyone lifted the glass, the wires would tug, the bells would ring, and the Warden Herons would come clattering up the stairs at the speed of an avalanche of cutlery. Tamsin asked in a whisper whether she could simply cut the wires, and Ilse, who knew a great deal about tension in thin lines, said that cutting would make them ring all the louder.

Ilse looked at the bells for a long time, and the beginnings of an idea unfolded slowly in her mind, like a map being opened. A bell that could not swing could not ring, she reasoned, and holding things still with a thread was precisely the sort of work that she did best in all the world. She had spent twelve years tying down loose corners, and now she would tie down twelve bells, and in the very same way.

Ilse took out her finest silk thread, cut twelve short lengths with a pair of scissors no bigger than a sparrow's beak, and asked Tamsin to hold the candle exactly still. Tamsin gripped it in both hands like a holy relic and promised, in a whisper, that she would not so much as sneeze for the next hour. The flame leaned, steadied and burned straight up like a small gold pencil, and then, with a quiet word to herself, Ilse began.

With fingers made steady by years of mending, Ilse slipped a loop of silk around the clapper of the first bell and drew it tight with a knot so small that it was hardly more than a rumour. The little silver shape trembled, shivered and settled, and not a whisper of sound came from it, and she let out a breath that she had been holding for a full minute. One down, she thought, with a trembling little thrill of triumph, and eleven more to go before the night was out.

A draught from some crack in the old stone set the fourth bell trembling on its wire, and the candle flame leaned over as if listening. Ilse caught the bell between two fingers a hair's breadth before it could swing, and held it perfectly still for what felt like an hour, until the air had settled and the flame stood upright again. She was almost surprised that her heart, which was beating so loudly in her ears, did not ring the other bells for her.

Bell by bell the work went on, and the minutes crawled past like snails across a wall, while the candle burned lower and the moon crept across the gap in the curtains. Tamsin, who could hardly bear the tension, held the light in both hands and bit her lip until it was nearly raw, yet she never allowed the flame to flicker. Ilse, bent over the ninth, tenth and eleventh bells in turn, was aware of nothing in the world except a thread and a clapper, and the next small knot.

With the steady fingers that had mended so many torn maps, Ilse tied a tiny knot around the clapper of the twelfth and final bell. It had taken her nearly an hour, and Tamsin, who could not have borne another minute of it, lowered the candle with trembling arms and let out a great shuddering sigh. The whole ring of bells hung as mute as pebbles, and the Moon Atlas lay waiting beneath its glass.

Ilse and Tamsin took hold of the glass cover on either side and lifted it together, as slowly as two snails climbing a wall. The wires tightened, the twelve silver bells swung against their silk, and not one of them uttered so much as a whisper. Tamsin set the glass down on the floor with infinite care, and they stood looking at each other as though they had just walked across a frozen lake.

Ilse undid the silver clasp, opened the great grey book and turned its heavy pages, one after another, with the reverence of a person handling a sleeping bird. Under the light of the candle every leaf was blank, as white and silent as new snow, and not so much as a coastline or a compass rose disturbed the whiteness. Tamsin's face fell like a loaf taken out of the oven too soon, and she muttered a word that Fenwick would never have allowed in his kitchen.

Tamsin whispered, in despair, that they had been tricked, and that after all this the book was only a pile of blank paper. Ilse touched the page, noticed its faint silvery sheen, and understood that the ink must wake only under the light of the moon, just as the sailors said. That was why the Harbour Lord opened the book at his window once a month, and why nobody else could ever read it.

Tamsin reached for the curtain to let in the moon, but Ilse caught her wrist and shook her head. From the outside the windows were mirrors, and a window that suddenly blazed with moonlight would flash across the water like a beacon to every patrol boat in the reef. They could neither read the book here nor stay to try, and she could feel the minutes slipping through her fingers like sand.

There was no time to copy anything, and a copy made by candlelight would have been blank in any case, so Ilse decided that the whole book must go with them. She closed the cover softly, fastened the silver clasp and told Tamsin that they would read it on the barge, under the open sky, where the moon could not be mistaken for a lamp. It was, she thought, the first theft of her whole life, and it was going to be an extremely heavy one.

Tamsin found a heavy cloth folded beneath the stand and they wrapped the Atlas in it, knotting the four corners together to make a sling with a loop on either side. The book weighed about as much as a small, sleeping dog, and the two of them lifted it between them with their elbows bent, like people carrying a very important pudding. They stood for a moment swaying beneath the weight, and then they began to move.

They had almost reached the door, their stockinged feet silent on the stone, when a lamp glowed beneath it and a deep, unhurried tread began to climb the stairs. It came with the tuneless humming of a man who is pleased with himself. It was Corvin Ashgrove, the Harbour Lord, who came as he always did on the night of the full moon to read the secrets of his book, and who was, by the sound of it, a full hour early.

Ilse and Tamsin dived behind the nearest heavy curtain with the Atlas hugged between them, praying that the velvet would not rustle and that the book would not suddenly sneeze. Behind the cloth, in the thickness of the wall, they found a narrow wooden door that Ilse recognised at once from a small cluster of holes on the thief's map. She laid a hand on Tamsin's arm and pointed, and Tamsin, to her eternal credit, did not ask a single question.

The Harbour Lord strode into the room with his velvet cloak swinging, set his lamp upon the floor and drew back the curtains one by one with the flourish of a conjuror. A flood of moonlight poured into the round room, the mirrored windows blazed silver, and the girls behind their curtain were suddenly two thin shadows in a world of white. He was humming a tune about a miller's daughter, which was, Ilse thought, a little hard to forgive.

While the Harbour Lord hummed and flourished at his window, Ilse eased open the narrow door and the two girls slid through it with the heavy bundle, onto a little stair that wound down into the darkness of the wall. She drew the door almost shut behind them, leaving a crack as thin as a thread, and held her breath. In the round room beyond, the tuneless humming stopped quite suddenly, and the silence that followed was a good deal worse than any noise.

Through the crack in the door Ilse watched the Harbour Lord stop dead in the middle of the room and stare at the empty stand and the glass cover lying on the floor. For a long moment he said nothing at all, and then his eyes travelled slowly along the ring of silent bells, each one tied round with its small, neat knot of silk. It was the first time she had ever seen her handiwork admired by a man who wished her at the bottom of the sea.

Then the Harbour Lord roared, with such fury that the glass trembled in its frames and the lamp flame leaned sideways, and the sound rolled down the stairwell like a boulder. Far below, in the great marble hall, a dozen mechanical herons snapped their heads up in perfect unison, their eyes blazing red, and began to stalk toward the stairs. He was shouting something about thieves, and walls, and an immediate search of every room.

The herons poured up the main stairs in a clattering river of brass, and the Harbour Lord stormed out of the round room to meet them, his cloak billowing behind him like the wing of a very angry bat. Ilse and Tamsin did not wait to see what happened next, but crept down the narrow stair in the thickness of the wall, as fast as they dared and a little faster. The sling bumped against Ilse's knees on every step, and she apologised to it each time.

The narrow stair ended at a small door behind a pillar in the corner of the great hall, and when Tamsin eased it open she found the vast room empty and white with moonlight. Every heron had rushed up the stairs in answer to the Harbour Lord's roar, leaving behind only a distant clatter and the long squares of black and white marble. It was the quietest the hall had been all night, and neither of them trusted it for a moment.

The two girls dashed across the polished marble in their stockinged feet, sliding and skating, with the heavy Atlas swinging between them like a pendulum. Halfway across Tamsin lost her footing and went down on one knee with a muffled yelp, and Ilse hauled her up by the elbow without dropping her side of the sling. They were running on the squares of the great marble board, and it seemed to Ilse that the whole game depended on whether they reached the edge.

Behind them the clattering suddenly changed its direction, as though a great clockwork tide had turned, and the herons wheeled round at the top of the short stair and came thundering back into the hall in a flood of brass. Their eyes burned red as hot coals, their long beaks stabbed the air, and their thin legs scissored across the marble at a speed that no girl in woollen socks could hope to equal. The two of them ran for the mouth of the main stairs with the Atlas bouncing between them.

They plunged down the spiral stairs with the Atlas between them, and the herons came after them with a noise like an avalanche of cutlery, a roar of brass on stone that filled the whole stairwell. Ilse counted the steps aloud as she ran, because counting was the only thing that kept her feet moving in the right order. The little lamp had gone out long ago, and the slits of moonlight in the wall flashed past like stripes on a zebra.

A pale chalk cross flashed out of the darkness on the wall, and Ilse screamed that this was it, the forty-first step, the false one, and gathered every ounce of strength in her legs. At the forty-first step she leapt, dragging Tamsin and the Atlas with her, and the three of them cleared the painted plank and landed in a heap on the one beneath. It was the most athletic moment of her whole life, and she was not even slightly proud of it.

The herons, which knew nothing of painted planks, charged straight onto the forty-first step and crashed through it in a bright cascade of brass, wings, legs and beaks tumbling over each other into the dark. A long splash echoed up from the depths, followed by a second, a third and a great many more, and then there was only the sound of the girls gasping for breath. For the first time that night the whole tower was perfectly still, and the girls were still alive, and the book was safe.

They tumbled down the last of the stairs, ran through the dark cellar past the island's stolen sacks, and crawled on hands and knees along the damp passage to the sea. Tamsin slammed the iron door behind them and jammed her spanner through the handle, and for good measure leaned her whole weight against it until the metal stopped shaking. Outside, the moon was high, the air was cold and sweet, and the girls had never felt so alive.

The two of them threw themselves into the little boat and rowed like people pursued by thunder, with the Atlas lying wrapped at their feet and their blistered hands forgotten. Behind them on the jetty a great lantern was being lowered into a fast black boat, and a voice they knew all too well bellowed across the water, demanding that they stop in the name of the Harbour Lord. Tamsin remarked, between strokes, that she had no intention of stopping in the name of anybody.

Ilse snatched up the signal lantern, steadied it against her knee and flashed it three times toward the open sea, with her hands shaking so badly that she nearly dropped it into the water. Far out beyond the rocks a single light winked back, as steady and as welcome as a star, and Tamsin let out a yelp of joy that carried a good deal farther than was wise. They bent to the oars with a new strength, because now they knew where they were going.

At the barge, Fenwick hauled the girls over the rail with one enormous hand apiece, and then he lifted the heavy bundle after them as lightly as a loaf of bread. Barnaby shouted from the bow that the tide was turning, which meant that they had very little time, and below decks Old Puffin began to roar like a happy dragon. Crumb the gull, perched on the mast, bowed his head in what looked remarkably like respect.

The whole crew began asking questions at once, and the answers flew round the deck in a tumble of herons, bells, thread, stairs and the Harbour Lord's astonished face. Fenwick wrapped the two girls in blankets and pressed hot tea into their hands, and Captain Brae touched Ilse's shoulder and said nothing at all, which was a good deal more than enough. Ilse drank, shivered and found that she was grinning like a person who has just been told the best joke in the world.

On the open deck, under a moon as round as a coin, Ilse set the Atlas on a barrel and opened it as slowly as a woman opening a letter that might change her life. The whole crew gathered round in a circle, Fenwick with his ladle in his fist and Tamsin with her chin on the barrel, and no one on the barge so much as breathed. Even the sea itself seemed to hold still, and the moon looked down from a sky without a single cloud.

The pages woke one by one with delicate lines of silver, as though invisible hands were drawing from beneath, and every channel of the Whisperreef bloomed before their eyes. There were arrows for the tide, tiny notes for every shoal, crescents for the places where the water ran fast, and a hundred small marks that no sailor had ever dreamed of. The crew gathered round in an awed circle, and not a single person trusted themselves to speak.

Barnaby, who could see none of it, leaned over the book with his face turned toward the moon, and a long and happy sigh escaped him. He said that he could smell the sea being made plain at last, as if somebody had opened a window in a room he had lived in all his life, and nobody laughed, for everyone knew what he meant. Ilse thought it was the loveliest thing that anyone had ever said about a map.

Turning the pages in the moonlight, Ilse found the Tide-Gate drawn in silver, with a tiny clock beside it showing the exact moment when the water would be lowest and the great doors would swing apart. It would open in about an hour, she calculated, and then stay open for a few minutes only, and then not again until the following night. The way to Kettle Island lay straight through it, and they would have to be waiting at the door.

A fast black boat slipped away from the jetty with a great lantern swinging at its bow, and Barnaby, who had heard it before anyone else, announced that it carried sixteen oars and a man who was extremely angry. Captain Brae called for every scrap of steam that Old Puffin possessed, and Tamsin, still wrapped in her blanket, dived into the engine room like a diver into the sea. The barge leaned forward and began to run, and the silver channels of the Atlas slid beneath their eyes.

The black boat was far quicker than the barge, and the water between them narrowed with every minute, until the lantern in its bow lit up the faces of the crew. By the time the moon was high the Harbour Lord was so close that Ilse could see the rings on his fingers as he cupped his hands to shout. He was smiling, which was far more frightening than all the roaring had been.

The Harbour Lord's voice carried across the water, as smooth as warm butter, and he offered Ilse a house in the best street in Lanternhaven, a salary beyond counting and the title of Chief Mapmaker. All that he asked in return, he said, was that she hand back the Atlas and forget the entire unfortunate affair. It was, Ilse thought, the most tempting offer she had ever heard, and also the most insulting.

The Harbour Lord added, in a tone of generous regret, that his clerk had torn up her licence notice that very morning, and that her little shop might remain open for as long as she cared to live. He spoke like a man who had never once been refused, and who had discovered that kindness costs nothing when one holds every card in the pack. Ilse noticed, with a small cold prickle, that he did not say a single word about Kettle Island or its hungry children.

For a long moment Ilse was truly tempted, because she could picture it all so clearly. A quiet study high in a tower, with endless supplies of ink and the finest paper in the world, a good door with three locks and not a heron or a tide in sight. It would be the life she had always thought she wanted, and she was astonished to find that it felt like a very small box.

Into her mind, uninvited, came a thin boy on Market Hill eating a bun as though he had not seen food for days, and then Mistress Pim's worried face over the counter. She thought of the children on Kettle Island, and of Captain Brae staring into the fire, and the quiet study in the tower seemed to shrink in her imagination until she could hardly see it. Some things, she discovered, are simply too heavy to be put in a box.

Ilse stood at the rail with the great book in her arms and, to her own surprise, spoke in a perfectly steady voice. A map, she said, is a promise to the next traveller, and nobody has the right to lock a promise in a tower and charge for it. She did not wait to hear his reply, but turned away and asked Barnaby for the next channel.

The smile dropped from the Harbour Lord's face like a plate from a shelf, and his voice, when it came again, was scarcely recognisable as the voice of a gentleman. He ordered his oarsmen to row harder, swore that no harbour in the world would ever take the barge again, and promised that Captain Brae would never captain so much as a rowing boat. Behind him the oars rose and fell in a furious white blur, and the black boat leapt forward as if it had been stung.

Barnaby tilted his head and announced that the gate was close, for he could smell the cold of its ancient stone and hear the water starting to draw back. Ilse bent over the Atlas, found the little silver clock beside the arch and worked out that the great doors would begin to open in less than a quarter of an hour. The black boat, meanwhile, had pulled so near that its lantern threw the barge's shadow across the water.

Tamsin pushed Old Puffin far beyond anything the little engine had ever been asked to do, and the steam screamed in every pipe like a choir of furious kettles. The barge leapt forward like a startled horse, her crooked mast groaning and her patched sides shuddering, while Fenwick shovelled coal until his shirt was black and his enormous arms were running with sweat. For the first time that night the black boat stopped gaining, and a ragged cheer went up from the crew.

Guided by the silver lines, the barge reached the Tide-Gate at the exact minute that the water had fallen low enough for the great arch to swing open. The two vast doors moved apart with a groan that shook the stones of the reef, and the moonlight poured through the widening gap like milk. Captain Brae, who had not breathed for some time, aimed the crooked bow at the very middle of it.

They shot through with an arm's length to spare, and behind them the old stones ground together with a boom that rolled across the whole reef, as though the sea itself had slammed a door. The Harbour Lord's boat, a heartbeat too late, was left drifting before a closed gate and a very long tide, with the lantern in her bow swinging uselessly in the dark. A faint and distant howl of rage reached them over the water, and Fenwick, grinning, tipped his hat to it.

Beyond the gate the sea lay calm and wide beneath the moon, and the Atlas showed a safe channel curving out round the outer edge of the reef, with not a single rock to trouble it. Ilse sat down beside the barrel to check it once more, and was asleep with the great book in her lap before she had reached the end of the page. Somebody laid a blanket over her shoulders, and somebody else, very gently, took her tea out of her hand.

At dawn the green hump of Kettle Island lifted out of the sea, wrapped in pink mist and circled by wheeling gulls, with a small grey town clinging to its southern slope. Fenwick woke Ilse with a mug of ginger tea, and she sat up blinking like an owl and stared at the place for which she had risked her door, her shop and the peace of a lifetime. It was smaller than she had expected, and far more beautiful, and it looked very much like somewhere that deserved to be saved.

At the end of the stone pier stood a crowd of thin, tired people, shading their eyes against the low sun, as still as the posts of the quay. They had seen no vessel for so long that for a while nobody dared to cheer, in case it was a mistake. Then someone recognised the crooked mast of the Gull's Patience, and the whole harbour began to shout.

Captain Brae leapt onto the pier before the barge had stopped moving and wrapped her arms around a small grey-haired woman in a patched shawl, lifting her clean off the ground. For a long time neither of them said a word, and the crowd on the quay, which had been shouting, fell quiet again out of pure tenderness. The great Captain Odalys Brae, Ilse saw, was crying openly into her mother's grey hair, and did not seem to care in the least who knew it.

Hester Brae was thin and tired, with hands as brown and knotted as old rope, but she was quite safe and so happy that she seemed to have grown an inch. Ilse, standing awkwardly on the deck with her hands clasped, discovered that her own eyes were wet, and had to look very hard at a seagull in order to recover. It was, she decided, an excellent seagull for the purpose, round and thoughtful and entirely uninterested in her.

Fenwick carried every sack of oats and flour from the barge onto the pier, lit a fire beneath the largest pot on the island and began to stir with a ladle the size of an oar. The thin children lined up with their bowls in a shy and silent queue, and they ate, and ate, and went back for more until their faces shone with butter. Nobody, Ilse noticed, had ever looked so completely happy as the big man stirring that pot.

Watching the busy quay, Ilse knew with a sudden, quiet certainty that a single book carried by a single barge could not feed a whole island. It must be copied for every boat and every captain, so that no one man could ever lock the reef again, and she must begin before the Harbour Lord had time to recover his temper. She went in search of a very large table, a great many candles and somebody who knew where the island kept its paper.

Ilse set up a table on the pier at moonrise, and the islanders, who understood at once, brought her sheets of paper, pots of ink and every candle they owned. Hester Brae knelt beside her with a bowl of crushed mother-of-pearl, which she stirred into the ink until it shimmered silver, and she explained that this was how the island had always made its best paint. Ilse looked at her in amazement and thought that Jory Lightfoot would have approved.

By midnight a dozen hands were helping her, and Ilse, who had never taught anything to anyone in her life, found that she was explaining the thief's code to a circle of net-menders with the patience of a village schoolmistress. Each of them was given one channel to copy, and Tamsin pricked the tiny feather marks with a pin. The first neat copy was drying in the wind on the quay, and it shone under the moon like a drift of silver feathers.

Within four days the islanders had produced hundreds of copies, each marked in careful silver ink and hung to dry from the rafters of the net loft like a flock of pale birds. A copy was tucked into the cabin of every fishing boat in the harbour, rolled in oilcloth and tied with a bit of string, and the old fishermen handled them as though they were holy. Ilse's hand ached, her back ached and her heart, to her considerable surprise, did not ache at all.

On the fifth morning a grain ship from the mainland, whose captain had heard the news, nosed carefully through the reef with a silver copy spread on her chart table. Her hold was full of flour and barley, and the whole island came down to the quay to carry sacks, even the smallest children, who dragged their share along the stones with grim and happy faces. Fenwick, standing in the middle of the crowd with a loaf in his arms, wept openly into the crust.

The fishing boats came home that evening with their nets heaving and their decks silver with fish, and the net-maker Joss Marlow, who laughed like a barrel rolling downstairs, could be heard across the whole harbour. Hester Brae pressed a parcel into Ilse's hands, and inside it lay a pair of thick grey socks knitted from island wool, still smelling faintly of the sheep. Every traveller, she said gravely, needs a spare pair, and Ilse tucked them into her bag with a feeling of unspeakable honour.

On the eighth day the Harbour Lord sailed into the island's little harbour with four guards and a face like thunder, and Clerk Dunnock hovering unhappily at his elbow with a bundle of papers. He demanded, in a voice that echoed off the green hills, that the stolen Atlas be handed over at once, and that the thieves be delivered to him at once. Nobody on the pier moved, and nobody spoke, and the gulls themselves seemed to hold their breath.

The islanders, hundreds strong and holding copies of the charts in their hands, simply stood shoulder to shoulder on the pier and said nothing. Old men, mothers with babies, fishermen with salt in their beards and children with silver ink on their fingers formed a wall that no guard cared to touch. It was, Ilse thought, the loudest silence she had ever heard in her whole quiet and careful life.

Ilse stepped forward, holding up one of her copies, and explained to the ship captains who had gathered on the quay that these charts were now in every cabin and could never be locked away again. Her voice, to her intense astonishment, did not tremble once, and she pointed out that a harbour fee which nobody could be made to pay was not a fee but a rumour. She added, for good measure, that the Harbour Lord's cellar was full of food that belonged to the island.

The captains conferred for a few moments in low and serious voices, and then, one after another, every hand went up in a vote to end the Harbour Lord's fee for ever. They further decreed that every sack, crate and barrel in his cellar should be returned to the island at his own expense, and they told him, with great politeness, to go home. It was, they all agreed afterward, the most enjoyable vote that any of them could remember.

Corvin Ashgrove looked at the crowd, looked at the paper in Ilse's hand, and understood at last that he had been outdrawn by a woman with a pot of paste. He opened his mouth, shut it again and turned on his heel, and the velvet cloak swept after him like a sulking cat. Behind him Clerk Dunnock paused at the rail, looked back at Ilse and, for the first time in his life, smiled.

When Ilse returned to Lanternhaven she found that the licence fee had been cancelled for every map shop in the city, and that her little street had hung out bunting in her honour. Mistress Pim flung her arms around her at the door, and neighbours she had never spoken to shook her hand and thanked her for something she scarcely understood. Ilse said that she had only done a bit of mending, and nobody believed her.

Ilse hung a new sign outside the shop, painted in her neatest hand, that said her maps were free to cross by, and then she went in and put the kettle on. Biscuit lay asleep on her best cushion with his paws folded like a pair of tiny gloves, and for the first time in her life she decided to let him stay. She settled at her desk with a pot of tea and a torn atlas that needed a gentle repair, and the rain began to patter at the window.

She had barely stirred in the sugar when the bell jangled and Captain Brae appeared in the doorway, grinning, with another brittle roll of paper under her arm. It had a feather in the corner, she said, and some very interesting holes in it, and she had only come to ask a small question. Ilse sighed deeply, put down her cup, and went to find her thickest socks.
